description: We're Orbit2Slope, a team of six engineering students from Daffodil International University, Bangladesh, bringing together computer science, software and electrical engineering. Landslides take lives in monsoon hills every year with little warning. Using NASA's NISAR radar data, we're building a way to warn communities earlier, starting at home and designed for the world.
summary:
Pahar Prohori (the Hill Guardian) is a landslide early warning system for six hills in Rangamati, Bandarban and Khagrachari. A sensor node on each hill reads soil moisture, ground acceleration, rainfall, humidity, temperature and wind. A Random Forest model scores every hill from those readings together with NISAR soil moisture and line-of-sight ground velocity. A hill turns DANGER only when the model's probability reaches 0.60, the ground soil is wet, and NISAR also shows wet soil or creep, so neither the sensors nor the satellite can raise the alarm alone.

That two-way check is our answer to "Dancing with the SARs". NISAR's L-band radar sees through monsoon cloud and picks up slow creep, but a pass comes roughly every 12 days, so it can tell you which slope is weakening, not that one is about to fail tonight. The node on the ground fills that gap.

The warnings people get today are based on rainfall and cover a whole district, so they say nothing about the slope above a particular house. Pahar Prohori warns hill by hill, in Bangla and English, with a spoken Listen button and road directions to the nearest shelter.
details:
The problem

Landslides hit the Chittagong Hill Tracts every monsoon, often at night and after days of rain. The warnings people get today are usually based on rainfall alone and cover a whole district. They say nothing about the particular slope above a house, so they are easy to ignore, and the next one is ignored too.

The challenge it answers

We built Pahar Prohori for the "Dancing with the SARs (NISAR)" challenge. NISAR's L-band radar sees through monsoon cloud and picks up slow ground creep and soil moisture. But a pass comes about every 12 days and processed data arrives later still, so NISAR can show which slopes are wet or moving, not that one is about to fail tonight. Sensors on the slope fill that gap. Pahar Prohori only raises its highest alert when both sources agree.

How it works

1. Ground. Each hill has a sensor node (CHT-NODE-01 to 06). Our Hill Guardian node uses a Raspberry Pi Pico W with a capacitive soil moisture sensor, a Hall effect water flow counter, an MPU6050 for tilt and vibration, a DHT11 and an anemometer, plus GPS and a GSM module. Nodes send readings to the backend through POST /api/ingest. The public demo replays a 7-day archive recorded at 10-minute steps.

2. Space. Every hill carries stored NISAR features: soil moisture (SME2-style), line-of-sight ground velocity in mm per month and radar coherence (GUNW-style), along with slope angle.

3. Model. A Random Forest uses 12 features: 8 from the recent sensor window (soil moisture now and its change, peak and mean acceleration, humidity, temperature, peak wind, rainfall total) and the 3 NISAR features plus slope. It outputs the chance of a landslide in the next 24 hours.

4. Decision. Each hill is SAFE, WATCH or DANGER. DANGER needs a probability of at least 0.60, ground soil moisture of at least 0.32 m3/m3, and NISAR confirming wet soil or creep. If any of these is missing, an elevated score stays at WATCH, so heavy rain alone never triggers DANGER. A DANGER alert holds for 24 hours with instructions in both languages.

What the app does

The Expo app runs on phones and on the web. The map shows all six hills colour-coded by status, with layers for risk, NISAR ground creep and soil moisture. Each hill page has live sensor tiles, 7-day charts and a rain outlook from Open-Meteo labelled with Bangladesh Meteorological Department rainfall categories. A 7-day replay re-runs the model hour by hour, so you can watch a hill move from SAFE to DANGER. The Listen button reads out the status and what to do, for people who cannot read well. Directions use real roads (OSRM on OpenStreetMap) to the nearest shelter, with live navigation and spoken turns in Bangla or English. A banner warns users when a DANGER hill is within 8 km. People can send hazard reports, the app keeps working offline from its last data, and phones get a notification for each new DANGER alert. The Live watch page shows the whole pipeline (sensors, NISAR, model, alerts) with per-hill node status.

Live demo: https://pahar-prohori-204-136-10-51.sslip.io

What is real and what is not yet

This is a research prototype, not an official warning service. The training set has 24,583 rows of satellite-style features (soil moisture, ground velocity, coherence), with sensor columns generated to follow them and labels set by hazard thresholds. That is why the model scores a ROC AUC of 1.0 on it: this number does not measure accuracy in the field. Rainfall total carries most of the model's weight (0.58), followed by soil moisture change (0.17) and NISAR soil moisture (0.11). The six per-hill NISAR values are placeholders in the units of the SME2 and GUNW products, not yet computed from downloaded granules, and the alert thresholds are experimental.

What we would build next

Collect verified landslide records alongside long-term sensor logs and retrain on real events. Automate the NISAR feed so new passes update each hill's features without manual work. Install physical nodes on the six hills in the 2027 monsoon, working with local disaster officials. Replace our 12 mapped shelters with the official shelter directory, and connect DANGER alerts to Bangladesh's 1090 emergency line and SMS, so warnings reach people who do not have a smartphone.
